The Beatles Preview Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) Take 2 From Rubber Soul Box Set

by Paul Cashmere on September 15, 2026

in New Music,News

The Beatles have released a third preview from the expanded Rubber Soul collection, revealing the previously unheard Second Version, Take 2 of Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown), featuring an early arrangement built around George Harrison’s sitar.

by Paul Cashmere

The Beatles have made a third recording available from the forthcoming Rubber Soul Special Edition, this time previewing the Second Version, Take 2 of Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown), an alternate studio performance that documents the development of the song and George Harrison’s early use of the sitar with The Beatles.

The recording is part of the expanded Rubber Soul collection due for release on 2 October 2026. The box set includes three different studio versions of Norwegian Wood, allowing listeners to follow the song’s progression from its first recorded form through to the arrangement that became the finished track.

The Take 2 version was recorded nine days after the first version, following The Beatles’ decision that the original performance was not satisfactory. The new recording has a substantially different opening to the released version, with double-tracked sitar playing the melody of the bridge before the song develops around John Lennon’s acoustic guitar, Paul McCartney’s bass and Ringo Starr’s drums.

The first version of what was then called This Bird Has Flown was recorded on the opening day of the Rubber Soul sessions. It featured Harrison playing the sitar, an instrument that had become a growing interest for the guitarist.

The Beatles returned to the song nine days later and recorded three further performances. On Second Version, Take 2, Lennon played acoustic guitar, McCartney bass and Starr drums, while Harrison supplied drone notes on sitar. Harrison added additional sitar parts to tracks two and three, with Lennon and McCartney’s vocals also recorded on track three.

The arrangement is notably different from the completed recording. Rather than beginning with an instrumental presentation of the verse melody, as the final version does, Take 2 opens with double-tracked sitar stating the tune of the bridge.

Harrison later explained the spontaneous nature of the instrument’s appearance on the song.

“It felt very familiar to me to listen to that music. Around that time I’d bought a cheap sitar in a shop called Indiacraft in London. When we were working on ‘Norwegian Wood’, it just needed something and it was quite spontaneous. I picked the sitar up and kind of found the notes. We put it on and it seemed to hit the spot and that was it.”

Harrison’s interest in Indian music developed during a period when The Beatles were expanding their musical vocabulary beyond conventional rock instrumentation.

He had first encountered the sound of the sitar while The Beatles were filming Help! and subsequently became increasingly interested in Indian music. A meeting with members of The Byrds in Los Angeles provided another important connection when David Crosby discussed the recordings of Indian sitar player Ravi Shankar with Harrison.

By the time Rubber Soul was being recorded, Harrison had acquired his own sitar in London. Norwegian Wood provided the opportunity to introduce its sound into a Beatles recording, establishing a musical direction that Harrison would explore further in the years that followed.

The sitar part on Norwegian Wood is therefore significant beyond this individual recording. It represents an early example of Harrison incorporating an instrument and musical influence from outside the Beatles’ established rock and pop framework.

Rubber Soul was originally released on 3 December 1965 after being recorded across October and November of that year. The album marked a major stage in The Beatles’ development, with Lennon, McCartney, Harrison and Starr working with increasingly sophisticated songwriting, arrangements and recording techniques.

Songs including Drive My Car, Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown), Nowhere Man, Michelle, Girl and In My Life demonstrated the group’s widening musical range. The album also preceded the more overt studio experimentation that would define Revolver and the later Beatles catalogue.

The 2026 Special Edition has been newly mixed by Giles Martin and Sam Okell from the original four-track master tapes. The expanded editions include the original mono mix, the US album configuration, new stereo and Dolby Atmos mixes, session recordings, home demos and the contemporary Day Tripper / We Can Work It Out single.

Among the previously unreleased material are the three versions of Norwegian Wood, making the song one of the clearest examples in the collection of The Beatles refining an arrangement in the studio.

The Second Version, Take 2 follows the release of earlier previews from the Rubber Soul Special Edition and adds another piece to the recording history surrounding one of the album’s most distinctive tracks.

The complete collection will be released on 2 October 2026 in multiple configurations, including Super Deluxe editions on four CDs and five LPs, as well as standard and Special Edition formats and a Blu-ray.
